claims.claim: The Martyrdom of Conon (BHG 361) is a Greek martyr account of the elderly gardener Conon, who lived near Magydos in Pamphylia in southern Asia Minor.
The Cult of Saints database says the Greek text was probably written in Pamphylia, probably in the 5th to 7th century.
The story is set in the persecution under Emperor Decius (249-251), and the Martyrdom of Conon has been studied as a source for that persecution.
The narrative opens after the deaths of the martyrs Papias, Diodorus and Claudian, when the governor comes to Magydos and finds the city and fields deserted because the locals have fled.
Guards led by a temple verger named Naodoros (also called Apelles), with a man called Origenes, search for Christians and find Conon watering an imperial garden at a place called Karmena.
Conon tells the governor he is from Nazareth and a relative of Christ, whom he worships as God over all.
The governor asks Conon only for a small offering of frankincense, wine and a branch with a brief prayer to Zeus, not a full sacrifice, and says he learned about Jesus from the Jews.

One article reads the Jewish origin of Conon as significant: it argues that lapsed Christians of Asia Minor often turned to Judaism, and that Conon served as a model of Christian apology in anti-Jewish polemic.
